newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish business worries about EMU without sterling.
newsitem.headline: Irish business worries about EMU without sterling.

text.p: The prospect of a single European currency going ahead without Britain is a serious worry for Irish industry which remains heavily dependent on sterling, Irish business leaders say.
If Ireland joins economic and monetary union (EMU) without Britain, they fear it will be highly exposed to sterling volatility without control over its exchange rate.
Economics professor Peter Neary said in a recent interview that Irish exporters hardest hit by a depreciating British pound would be primarily small companies.

"The main question is what type of firms will suffer (if sterling falls). I believe they will be disproportionately small, disproportionately Irish-owned and disproportionately labour intensive," Neary said.
Ireland's official trade statistics show a sharp reduction in economic dependence on Britain over the last 25 years, but the statistics do not show the whole story.

In 1970, 66 percent of Irish exports went to Britain with only 12 percent going to the rest of Europe. In 1995, official trade data showed only 26 percent of Irish exports were destined for Britain and 47 percent to the rest of Europe.
The problem is the statistics are skewed by multinational transactions.

Multinational corporations currently account for half of all exports out of Ireland. These large transnational operations use Ireland as a backdoor to Europe and have little trade with Britain. This makes Ireland's dependence on Britain look artificially low.
The bulk of indigenous Irish manufacturing exports are still going to Britain and their dependence on sterling is great.
So why does Ireland not take a risk averse view and follow the route of Britain, which has secured an opt out from monetary union and has yet to decide whether to join the single currency project.
Ireland has made many attempts to break its dependence on its former colonial ruler. It decoupled from sterling, breaking its one-to-one link, in 1989.
Since then Ireland has made great efforts to be a "good European", struggling to keep the Irish currency at a credible level within the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).
The Irish government has remained unwavering in its intra-party unity over EMU and has kept the economic criteria for membership set out in the Maastricht Treaty high on its fiscal agenda.
While most European Union aspirants struggle to meet EMU entry requirements, Ireland has no such problem.
Its economy is booming. For the last four years, Ireland has boasted the fastest growth rate in Europe.
Its gross domestic product (GDP) growth rate hit double digits in 1995, running at 10.7 percent year-on-year. This compares with an average EU growth rate of roughly two percent.

Although concerns about joining Europe without Britain have become more vociferous, a recent survey of Irish business still showed a general acceptance that Ireland would be worse off it it stayed out of EMU with Britain than if it entered without Britain.

"If Ireland was to stay outside EMU it is arguable that we could be in a vulnerable and isolated position," Ireland's central bank governor Maurice O'Connell told the recent European Finance Convention in Dublin.
"The markets would question our motives. The Irish pound might carry a significant interest rate premium," he said.
Staying out could also impact on inward investment, he warned.
"One has to ask whether an Ireland semi-detached from the heart of Europe would remain such an attractive location for new overseas investment."
O'Connell felt that Ireland may find it considerably more difficult down the road to satisfy EMU criteria. "These are serious downsides that we should not underestimate."
Finance minister Ruairi Quinn has articulated similar concerns.

"If we were to be outside the euro and declared to the rest of the world that we were qualifying to join a single currency but we were deciding for whatever reason not to join it, largely because of our dependence on sterling, I think we would compound our vulnerability," Quinn told Reuters in a recent interview.
